section.title: The Army and the Day of the LORD
section.sectionRationale: The locusts of chapter one now swell into a terrifying army marching under the LORD's own command. Joel sounds the alarm from Zion: the Day of the LORD is not merely near, it is arriving, a day of darkness before which the earth quakes and the heavens tremble. This is the darkest note of the book, and it sets up the sudden turn to mercy that follows.
section.thesis: The Day of the LORD comes as an unstoppable army led by God Himself, great and very dreadful, so that the only honest question left is, who can endure it, a question the next movement will answer with a call to return.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the trumpet of alarm and the day of darkness; the relentless, disciplined advance of the army; and the LORD raising His voice at the head of His camp, leaving the reader with the question, who can endure it.

units.label: Sound the alarm, the day is near

verses.text: Blow the {{shofar|ram’s horn}} in Zion; sound the alarm on My holy mountain! Let all who dwell in the land tremble, for the {{yomYHWH|Day of the LORD}} is coming; indeed, it is near.

a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness. Like the {{shachar|dawn}} overspreading the mountains a great and strong army appears, such as never was of old, nor will ever be in ages to come.
Before them a fire devours, and behind them a flame scorches. The land before them is like the Garden of Eden, but behind them, it is like a desert wasteland; surely nothing will escape them.
Their appearance is like that of horses, and they gallop like swift steeds.
With a sound like that of chariots they bound over the mountaintops, like the crackling of fire consuming stubble, like a mighty army deployed for battle.
Nations writhe in horror before them; every face turns pale.
They charge like mighty men; they scale the walls like men of war. Each one marches in formation, not swerving from the course.
They do not jostle one another; each proceeds in his path. They burst through the defenses, never breaking ranks.
They storm the city; they run along the wall; they climb into houses, entering through windows like thieves.

units.label: The LORD at the head of His army

verses.text: Before them the earth quakes; the heavens tremble. The sun and moon grow dark, and the stars lose their brightness.

The LORD raises His voice in the presence of His army. Indeed, His camp is very large, for mighty are those who obey His command. For the Day of the LORD is great and very dreadful. Who can endure it?

shofar.gloss: A ram's horn trumpet, blown to summon assemblies, warn of danger, and mark sacred moments. Here it is the alarm of war, calling all of Zion to tremble and take shelter before the advancing Day. The same horn that sounds terror in chapter two will sound the call to a holy fast a few verses later, warning and gathering in one blast.

yomYHWH.gloss: The Day of the LORD, Joel's central theme. It is the appointed time when God comes in power to judge and to save, here portrayed as a day of darkness, gloom, and dread. In this passage the Day arrives as an overwhelming army under God's own command, and the darkening of sun, moon, and stars marks it as more than any ordinary battle.

shachar.gloss: The dawn, the first light spreading across the mountains. Joel uses it not for hope but for dread: like the dawn the army spreads unstoppably over the hills, vast and unavoidable. The image captures how the Day of the LORD advances, inevitable and covering everything in its path.

basic.context: The locust swarm of chapter one now becomes a full army on the march, described like cavalry and soldiers scaling walls. Joel commands the trumpet to be blown from Zion to warn everyone. This is the Day of the LORD arriving, a day of thick darkness, and the LORD Himself is leading the army. The passage ends with a chilling question: who can endure it?
basic.hermeneutics: Joel piles up simile after simile, the army is like horses, like chariots, like fire, like mighty men, to overwhelm the reader with dread on purpose. Whether the army is the locusts intensified, a coming human invader, or the final judgment, the aim is the same: to make the Day feel real and near so the people will not stay complacent.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter opens with the shofar, the ram's horn, sounding the alarm of war. The army spreads like the shachar, the dawn, unstoppable across the mountains. And the Day of the LORD, yom YHWH, is not just near now but coming, arriving, great and very dreadful.
basic.typology: The darkening of sun, moon, and stars becomes a fixed picture of the Day of the LORD that Jesus takes up when He describes His return, Matthew 24:29. The unstoppable army under God's command foreshadows the final judgment. And the terrifying question, who can endure it, finds its answer only in the One who endured the Day in our place.
basic.christ: The passage leaves us with a question we cannot answer on our own: who can endure the Day of the LORD? No one can, by strength or merit. Jesus is the answer, the One who faced the full darkness of that Day at the cross, who endured the judgment so that all who shelter in Him will be able to stand. He turns the trumpet of terror into the trumpet of salvation.
basic.god: God is not a distant spectator of judgment; He leads the army in person, His voice thundering at its head. This shows His total sovereignty, even the instruments of judgment obey His command. It also shows His holiness: the Day is dreadful precisely because God is holy and sin is serious. Yet the very warning is mercy, sounding the alarm before the blow falls.
basic.crossReferences: The Day of darkness echoes Amos 5 and Zephaniah 1. The darkened sun, moon, and stars are picked up by Jesus in Matthew 24 and in Revelation 6. The trumpet of alarm anticipates the trumpet of the last day, 1 Corinthians 15:52.
basic.oneStory: This dark chapter is a warning shot in the long story of the Day of the LORD. It makes the danger vivid so that mercy will be all the sweeter. The question it raises, who can endure it, drives the whole Bible toward Jesus, who endured the Day so His people never will.

context.literary:
This section is built as a battle alarm in three stages, and each stage widens the frame. Verses 1 and 2a are the call: a horn, a cry and a trembling land. Verses 2b to 9 are the advance, a close-up of the invader from the front line to the rooftops. Verses 10 and 11 pull the camera back to the sky and to the Commander. The movement is from the local to the cosmic, and from the army to the One who leads it.

The section is framed by trembling. In verse 1 all who dwell in the land 'tremble,' and in verse 10 the earth quakes and the heavens tremble, using the same Hebrew root. What begins as a human fear ends as the shaking of creation. A second frame is the phrase 'Day of the LORD' at the opening and the close, and the last occurrence adds two adjectives, 'great and very dreadful,' so that the reader enters the poem with a warning and leaves it with a verdict.

The middle of the poem is a catalogue of motion. Verse 3 sets fire in front and flame behind, verses 4 and 5 bring horses, chariots and stubble in a blaze, verses 7 and 8 describe warriors who do not swerve or jostle, and verse 9 takes them over the walls and through the windows. The poetry has no rest, because the advance itself has none. Compare the way Proverbs 30:27 observes that locusts have no king and yet march in formation. The orderliness that Joel stresses in verses 7 and 8 is the unnerving part of the description.

A deliberate echo links this passage to the previous chapter. The locusts that consumed in chapter 1 now arrive as an army, and the phrase 'such as never was of old, nor will ever be in ages to come' in verse 2 recalls the language used of the locusts of Exodus 10:14, where nothing like them had been seen before or would be again. The opening of the verse, 'a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness,' repeats Zephaniah 1:15 word for word. The passage ends on a question and not a resolution, and the hinge that follows in verse 12, 'Yet even now,' is held back so that the dread can sink in first.
context.historical:
The ram's horn was the alarm of ancient Israel. Numbers 10:1 to 10 distinguishes the signals: long blasts convened the assembly, and short blasts sounded the alarm for war or for the camps to set out. Joel's first verse calls for the alarm, and the setting is Zion, which the LORD calls 'My holy mountain.' The trumpet is blown in the city of the temple, and the alarm is raised by the priests whose ministry had been interrupted in chapter 1. Amos 3:6 asks the nation whether the people can hear a horn in the city and not tremble.

The Day of the LORD was a theme that the prophets inherited and turned on its head. Amos had warned those who longed for the day that it would be darkness and not light, Amos 5:18 to 20, which suggests that the people thought of it as a day when the LORD would fight for them. Joel makes clear that the army of the day is the LORD's own and that Zion is the first place it will be felt. The phrase 'such as never was of old' would have sounded to Israel's ears as a pointer to the Exodus, where they had seen an army of locusts and learned who God was.

The picture of the advance matches what was known of both locusts and armies. Locusts do move in order, as Proverbs 30:27 observes. Armies of the day, Assyrian and later Babylonian, scaled walls and broke into cities, and the picture of the invaders 'entering through windows like thieves' recalls Jeremiah 9:21, where death climbs in through the windows. The reader in Judah would have known both kinds of threat, and the poem does not need to choose between them in order to frighten.

The Eden comparison in verse 3 would have been understood by anyone who knew Genesis. The land before the army is like the Garden of Eden, and behind it is a desert wasteland. Genesis 13:10 had called the well watered plain of the Jordan like the garden of the LORD, and Ezekiel 36:35 would say that a desolate land had become like the Garden of Eden. In every case Eden is the picture of a land at its richest, and Joel uses it to show how much is lost.
context.canonical:
Joel 2 draws on the older prophets and is drawn on by the later ones. The opening description of the Day is nearly a quotation of Zephaniah 1:14 to 16, where the 'great Day of the LORD' comes with horn blast and battle cry, as 'a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness.' The thick cloud and darkness also recall Sinai, where the people stood at the foot of the mountain under 'black clouds and deep darkness,' Deuteronomy 4:11. Joel therefore sets the Day beside the day God revealed Himself on the mountain, and the fear of the nation at Sinai is renewed. The question at the end of the passage appears again in Malachi 3:2, 'who can endure the day of His coming? And who can stand when He appears?'

Joel's book itself carries these lines forward. Joel 3:14 to 16 repeats the darkening of sun and moon and has the LORD roar from Zion, and Amos 1:2 begins with the same roar. Joel 2:28 to 32, just beyond this passage, promises the outpouring of the Spirit and deliverance for everyone who calls on the name of the LORD, which Peter quotes at Pentecost, Acts 2:16 to 21, and Paul in Romans 10:13.

The New Testament takes up the cosmic signs of verses 10 and 11. Jesus says that after the tribulation the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light and the powers of the heavens will be shaken, Matthew 24:29. Revelation 6:12 to 17 describes the sixth seal with the sun black like sackcloth and ends with the cry of those who ask who is able to withstand the great day. Revelation 9:7 to 9 describes locust-like creatures that look like horses prepared for battle, with the sound of many chariots, in a clear echo of Joel 2:4 and 5. Peter says that the Day of the Lord will come like a thief, 2 Peter 3:10, as Paul does in 1 Thessalonians 5:2, which may recall the thieves of verse 9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Joel wanted his hearers to stop treating the Day of the LORD as someone else's problem. The first chapter had said the Day was near. This chapter says it is coming, and it puts the evidence in front of them with the urgency of a watchman on the wall. The aim is not to give a timetable but to make a settled people tremble, as the text says, and to make them ready to hear the call to return in the verses that follow.

He also wanted them to grasp who stands behind the army. The shock of verse 11 is that the voice at the head of the host is the LORD's. This turns the whole picture. Israel had been trained to think of the LORD as the one who fights against their enemies, and Joel tells them that He can also lead an army against His own city. It is a text that unseats false security, and it makes the sort of pride that says 'it cannot happen here' impossible.

The closing question was meant to be left open. 'Who can endure it?' presses the hearers to the edge of despair, and that is where the next verses begin. The author uses the dread as the doorway to grace. If the hearer is not afraid, the offer of mercy in verse 12 has no pull, but if he is, the same God who frightened him is the one he can run to.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes what will happen when the Day of the LORD arrives, and it prescribes only the alarm: blow the horn, sound the warning, let the land tremble. Nothing here tells believers to launch an invasion or to look for particular events on the news and read them as this army. The movement of armies in later history has often led readers to name the invaders in Joel, and the habit has a poor record. The text's own concern is the community's readiness.

What does carry across is the call to take warnings seriously. The prophet's task is to sound an alarm that others may prefer not to hear, and the church has a similar duty to proclaim that there is a coming Day. The New Testament joins the warning to hope, so that Paul can say in 1 Thessalonians 5:4 and 5 that believers are not in darkness for the Day to surprise them as a thief.

The graphic descriptions of the army and the cosmic signs are in the poetic style of prophecy. The text uses simile after simile, 'like horses,' 'like chariots,' 'like fire,' and a careful reader will not turn them into a precise forecast of equipment. They are there to convey what cannot be pictured, the weight of a day when the LORD acts.

debates.question: Who or what is the army of Joel 2?

views.label: A more terrible locust plague
views.case: The passage keeps the images of chapter 1, and the likeness to horses and the formation of the march fit locusts, as Proverbs 30:27 notes. The description of leaping over mountaintops, eating before and behind, and entering windows suits a swarm, and the Eden and wasteland contrast of verse 3 fits the way locusts leave a land bare. Joel 2:25 later calls the locusts 'My great army that I sent against you.'

views.label: A human army, perhaps Assyrian or Babylonian
views.case: The language of warriors, walls, charge and formation is the language of war, and the footnote at verse 4 allows 'cavalry' or 'charioteers.' Many see the locusts as a prelude and the army as the human invader that the Day brings, the 'northern army' of verse 20. The armies of the great empires scaled walls and took cities.

views.label: An eschatological host of the final Day
views.case: Because the cosmic signs and the language of 'never was of old, nor will ever be' have no ordinary parallel, others read the army as the final judgment host, to which the prophets point and which Revelation takes up. In this case Joel's present crisis and the last Day are made to overlap.

debates.bearing: The poem keeps the three readings in tension on purpose. Whether locusts, soldiers or an end-time host, the army is the LORD's, verse 11, and the right response is the same. A reader does best to hold the near and far fulfilments together and not force a single identification where the text itself has blended them.

debates.question: Is the Day of the LORD past, present or future in Joel?

views.label: An imminent historical event
views.case: The language of nearness in 1:15 and 2:1, and the clear link to a present plague, suggest that the Day is being applied to the people's own time as a visitation of judgment on Judah. Other prophets use the same phrase of historical judgments, as Ezekiel 30:2 and 3 does of Egypt.

views.label: The final, end of the age Day
views.case: The cosmic signs, the shaking of the heavens and the stars losing their brightness point beyond any single historical event. Jesus uses the same language of His return, Matthew 24:29, and the New Testament treats the Day as still ahead.

views.label: A recurring pattern with a final goal
views.case: A third view holds that the Day of the LORD is any time God acts decisively in judgment and salvation, with historical visitations pointing toward the last one. On this reading both earlier views are true at once.

debates.bearing: The New Testament's use shows that the Day was not exhausted by one historical event. Peter at Pentecost can quote Joel as fulfilled and still speak of a coming Day, Acts 2:20 and 2 Peter 3:10. The wise reader will take the near warnings seriously and keep the final Day in view.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verse gives two commands for sound. 'Blow' is taqa, the ordinary verb for sounding a horn, and 'sound the alarm' is a form of the verb ruaʿ, from the noun teruah, the shout or the short blast. The distinction is the one made in Numbers 10:5 to 9, where long blasts gather the assembly and short blasts raise the alarm and call the camps to move. The pairing in Joel asks for both: a summons to the assembly and the cry of war. The reader should hear the whole nation being called together under threat.

The verb 'tremble' in verse 1 is ragaz, and it returns in verse 10 for the quaking of the earth. It is the shaking of a person or a place under fear or force, and the repetition says that the land's trembling at the horn is the beginning of the heaven and earth's trembling at the army. In verse 6 the nations 'writhe' with a related image of birth pangs.

The description of the day in verse 2 stacks four nouns in pairs, choshek and afelah, anan and arafel, darkness and gloom, cloud and blackness. The second pair is the one used for the thick cloud of Sinai in Deuteronomy 4:11, and the whole line is word for word the line of Zephaniah 1:15. Joel is not inventing the description but quoting a prophetic tradition, and the use of the language of Sinai gives it the weight of a theophany: the LORD is about to appear.

The statement that nothing like this has been 'of old' or will be 'in ages to come' echoes the formula of Exodus 10:14, where the locusts were of a size never seen before or after. The Hebrew 'olam, translated 'of old,' marks a far horizon, and 'generation to generation' for the future completes the sweep. The same measure is used in Exodus 11:6 of the cry in Egypt. Joel puts this army in the company of the plagues.

In verse 3 the fire and the flame 'devour' and 'scorch,' and the first verb is the common Hebrew verb to eat, the same one used for the work of the locusts in chapter 1. The land is said to be 'like the Garden of Eden,' gan eden, in front and 'a desert wasteland,' midbar shemamah, behind. The word shemamah is the noun for desolation, used of land left empty after a catastrophe. The pairing of Eden and desolation places the army as an agent of reversal, since it undoes what the LORD planted.

Verse 4 describes the appearance of the army as 'like horses' and the footnote notes that the word can be read as horsemen or cavalry. The word in verse 5 for 'chariots' is merkavot, and the comparison to the 'crackling of fire consuming stubble' is the sound of the locusts' wings, as Revelation 9:9 describes it, a sound like many horses and chariots rushing into battle.

In verse 9 the invaders enter 'through windows like thieves.' The word for thief is gannav, and the picture of death entering by windows is also found in Jeremiah 9:21. The windows are the weak points of a house, and the picture is of an enemy that finds the one unguarded opening.

Verse 10 says the sun and moon 'grow dark,' using the verb qadar. It is the same verb that describes a person in black mourning dress or bowed down with grief, as in Psalm 35:14. The luminaries are pictured as mourners.

Finally, in verse 11 the LORD 'raises His voice,' literally gives His voice, and the army is called 'His camp.' Those who 'obey His command' are literally those who do His word, the description Psalm 103:20 uses for the mighty angels who carry out His word. 'Dreadful' is nora, the word of fear that Malachi 4:5 uses of the same Day, and the verb behind 'endure' in the question is from the root kul, which Malachi 3:2 also uses in its question about the Day.

typology.type: The sun, moon and stars darkened, Joel 2:10
typology.fulfillment: The darkening of the heavens is the sign of the Day. At the death of Jesus, darkness came over the whole land from the sixth hour until the ninth, Matthew 27:45, and the prophet Amos had said that the LORD would make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight, Amos 8:9. The correspondence is that the Day of the LORD's wrath fell, in a first installment, on the Son at the cross. Jesus also takes the language for His return, Matthew 24:29. The type falls short in that the darkness of Calvary lasted three hours and ended in the cry 'It is finished,' while the final signs usher in the end of the age.

typology.type: The LORD at the head of His army, Joel 2:11
typology.fulfillment: The commander who speaks before the host is the LORD Himself. Joshua met a man before Jericho who said, 'I have now come as Commander of the LORD's army,' Joshua 5:14, and Joshua fell on his face. In the New Testament the rider on the white horse leads the armies of heaven, Revelation 19:11 to 14, and His name is the Word of God. The correspondence is that the LORD leads His forces and is not merely behind them. The escalation is that the Commander is identified as Christ. The type falls short because Joel's army is an instrument of judgment on Judah, while the army of Revelation 19 comes after the Lamb has already been slain.

The ram's horn warns of the coming Day. In the New Testament the trumpet sounds again at the end, so that Paul writes that at the last trumpet the dead will be raised imperishable, 1 Corinthians 15:52, and that the Lord Himself will descend with the trumpet call of God, 1 Thessalonians 4:16. The correspondence is that the alarm is a signal that the Day has come. For those in Christ the final trumpet is a sound of deliverance, whereas in Joel it is a sound of dread. The type falls short in that Joel's trumpet could only warn, while the last trumpet accomplishes what it announces.

typology.type: The thieves in the windows, Joel 2:9
typology.fulfillment: The invaders enter houses like thieves, unseen and at an unguarded point. The picture is a minor one in Joel, but Jesus uses a thief in the night to teach watchfulness, Matthew 24:43 and 44, and Paul and Peter say that the Day of the Lord comes the same way, 1 Thessalonians 5:2 and 2 Peter 3:10. The correspondence is the suddenness. This should be taken as an echo and not as a prediction, since Joel does not use the picture for the Day itself. The correspondence falls short because the image in Joel is of a threat to be feared, while in the Gospels it is a reason for a believer to be ready.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first through the question it leaves hanging. 'Who can endure it?' is a question about the Day of the LORD, and Malachi 3:2 asks it again, 'who can endure the day of His coming? And who can stand when He appears?' The New Testament's response is not that someone strong enough can stand, but that someone has stood in the Day for others. Revelation 6:17 echoes the cry, 'who is able to withstand it?', and the very next chapter sees a multitude standing before the throne and before the Lamb, Revelation 7:9 to 14. They stand because they have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb. Paul says that through Christ 'we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we now stand,' Romans 5:2, and that we will be saved from God's wrath through Him, Romans 5:9.

It leads to Christ through the darkness. The signs of verse 10 have a first fulfilment in a place Joel could not have named. When Jesus hung on the cross, darkness fell over the whole land from noon until three, Matthew 27:45. A reader should not claim that Joel predicted this, but the New Testament gives us enough to say that the wrath of the Day was borne at Calvary. Where Joel's hearers feared a Day of darkness, the Gospels record that the Son went into it. The words 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?', Matthew 27:46, are the sound of a person standing in the Day on behalf of others.

It leads to Christ through the Commander. Verse 11 says that the LORD raises His voice before His army, and the New Testament identifies the One at the head of the heavenly armies as Christ. In Revelation 19:11 to 16 the rider on the white horse judges and makes war in righteousness, and on His robe is written 'King of kings and Lord of lords.' The Day of the LORD is the Day of the Lord Jesus, and Paul says the same, speaking of 'the day of our Lord Jesus Christ,' 1 Corinthians 1:8. That is the strongest christological point of the passage: the Day that frightened Israel has the Messiah at its centre.

It leads to Christ through the offer that follows. Verse 12 will say that even now the LORD invites a return, and the promise attached to it, which Peter and Paul both quote, is that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved, Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13. Paul reads 'the LORD' there as Jesus, Romans 10:9 to 13. The trumpet that sounds terror in chapter 2 sounds salvation for those who call on Him.

A caution is needed. The army is not a picture of Christ and the locusts do not represent anything in His life. The passage supplies the dread and the unanswered question, and the New Testament answers by showing who stands in the Day. A reader who forces details such as the horses and thieves into the Gospels goes beyond what the text supports.
study.god:
The passage shows that the LORD is the commander of every army. The most startling line in the poem is that the one who raises His voice before the host is God. The army is called 'His camp,' and its soldiers are 'those who obey His command.' The Bible does not teach a God who is a spectator at the great movements of history. Even instruments that do not know Him, as Isaiah 10:5 says of Assyria, go where they are sent. This is a hard doctrine, and it is meant to give the faithful a basis for hope as much as the unfaithful a reason for fear, since no power on earth is outside the reach of His voice.

It shows Him as a God who takes sin seriously. The terror of the Day is not the temper of a God who has lost control but the response of One whose holiness cannot ignore evil. The shaking of the heavens, the darkening of the sun, and the question of who can endure are all ways of saying that the Judge of all the earth does right, Genesis 18:25. A God who could not be dreaded would also not be worth trusting, because He would not care about justice.

It shows Him as one who gives warning. The chapter opens with a horn, and a horn is a gift to those who hear it. The LORD does not strike without a sign, and here He has a watchman blow the alarm on His holy mountain. Amos 3:7 says that the Lord God does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets, and Joel is an example. The alarm is mercy in a form that sounds like threat.

It shows Him as the Creator, whose creation responds to Him. The earth quakes, the heavens tremble, the sun and moon darken. The universe is not a neutral stage but a creation that answers to its Maker's voice. What He spoke into being, Genesis 1:3 and 14, He can shake.

It shows the tension that runs through the book. The same God who leads the army is the one who, in the next verse, says 'return to Me with all your heart,' and who is 'gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion,' Joel 2:13. The dread is not the opposite of that character but one of its expressions. His patience has an end, and a patient God warns before He acts.

For worship, the passage teaches reverence. The church can easily lose the sense of the weight of God, and Joel recovers it. We are taught to hear the horn, to hold together the fear of the LORD and trust in Him, and to ask the question 'who can endure?' in a way that sends us to the One in whom we can. It also teaches us that a message of judgment can be a work of kindness, because a warning is given only to those who can still respond.

crossReferences.note: The great Day of the LORD is near, a day of darkness and gloom, clouds and blackness, of horn blast and battle cry. The language is almost word for word the language of Joel 2:1 and 2. The two prophets draw on one tradition of the Day, in which the LORD Himself comes in war.

Amos warns those who long for the Day of the LORD that it will be darkness and not light. His warning shows that Israel had treated the Day as a vindication, and Joel presses the same point by showing the LORD leading an army against Zion.

The plague of locusts on Egypt was one such as never was before and never will be again. Joel 2:2 uses the same measure of an army of locusts, which places the coming Day in the line of the great acts of God in the Exodus.

The law distinguishes the long blast that gathers the assembly from the short blasts of the alarm for war. Joel's double command in verse 1, blow and sound the alarm, draws on this practice and calls the whole community to prepare.

At Sinai the people stood under a mountain blazing with fire, with black clouds and deep darkness. The darkness and cloud of Joel 2:2 recall that day, which suggests that the Day of the LORD is a new appearance of the God who spoke at the mountain.

Death has climbed in through our windows and entered our fortresses. Joel's invaders enter houses through windows, and the same picture in Jeremiah shows how the prophets spoke of judgment as something that reaches into the places people thought were safe.

The angels are mighty in strength, carrying out His word and hearkening to the voice of His command. The language is close to Joel's description of those who obey the LORD's command in verse 11, which suggests that His army is a heavenly host as well as a human one.

'Who can endure the day of His coming? And who can stand when He appears?' Malachi asks the question of Joel 2:11 in nearly the same words, and goes on to answer that He will be like a refiner's fire, so that the question is about being purified.

Jesus says the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. He takes the cosmic signs of Joel 2:10 and applies them to His own return, and so claims the Day of the LORD as His own.

At the sixth seal the sun goes black and the moon turns red, and the people cry out, 'who is able to withstand it?' The cry in Revelation takes the question of Joel 2:11 and sets it at the opening of the final judgment, and the next chapter shows who stands.

The locusts of the abyss look like horses prepared for battle, with the sound of wings like chariots rushing into battle. John uses the imagery of Joel 2:4 and 5 to describe a plague at the end, showing how Joel's pictures became a pattern for later prophecy.

The Day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. Paul takes up the language of the Day and applies it to believers, telling them they are children of the light and need not be surprised, so that Joel's warning becomes a call to watchfulness.

study.oneStory:
The Bible has already told the story of one army sent by God. In Genesis 6 the flood came as a judgment on a world that was full of violence, and in Exodus God brought plagues on Egypt, with the locusts among them. Joel 2 takes that pattern and turns it on Zion. The book's central concern is not a single plague but the repeated movement of Scripture in which the LORD comes to judge and to save, and this chapter is the place where the movement becomes a name, the Day of the LORD.

What it answers from earlier is the confidence of a people who believed that the covenant meant they were safe. Amos had already said that this belief was a delusion, and Joel presses it by describing the LORD leading an army against His own city. The chapter also answers the Eden story. The garden that was lost in Genesis 3 appears here as a picture of what the army destroys, and the land that was like Eden becomes a desert. It is the curse of Genesis working itself out in the history of a nation.

What it sets up is the hinge of verse 12, where the book turns from threat to invitation, and then the promise of restoration and of the Spirit. The question 'who can endure it?' is not left to hang. The prophets after Joel carry the Day forward, Malachi asks the question again, and the New Testament shows that a Man has stood in the Day.

The story comes to rest in Christ, who endures the darkness on the cross and who will return as the Commander of the armies of heaven. Pentecost, with its wind and fire, shows that the Day has begun to break into history in the form of the Spirit poured out, and the last trumpet will complete what the first trumpet at Zion began. Those who call on the name of the Lord are saved, which is the gospel's way of answering the question.

The new creation is the final answer. Revelation 21:1 and 2 describes a new heaven and earth in which the sea is gone and the holy city comes down from God, and 21:4 says that there will be no more mourning or crying or pain. The Eden of Joel 2:3 is not lost forever. The desert behind the army is replaced by a garden city with a river and a tree of life, Revelation 22:1 and 2, and the Day that began with a trumpet ends with the voice from the throne saying, 'It is done.'

quiz.q: How does chapter 2 relate to the locust plague of chapter 1?

options.text: It intensifies it: the swarm is now portrayed as an unstoppable army arriving on the Day of the LORD.
options.note: Joel heightens the plague into military imagery tied to the Day of the LORD.

options.text: It describes a completely different disaster unrelated to the locusts.
options.note: The army continues and heightens the locust imagery of chapter one.

options.text: It looks back on the plague as something already over and resolved.
options.note: The plague informs the picture, but Joel presents the Day as coming, not past.

options.text: It cancels the earlier warning and says there is no danger.
options.note: The danger is escalated, not cancelled.

quiz.q: Who is leading the army in this passage?

options.text: The LORD Himself, who raises His voice at the head of His camp.
options.note: Verse 11 makes God the commander of the host on the Day of the LORD.

options.text: A foreign emperor whose forces God merely permits.
options.note: Human agents may be involved, but the text names the LORD as the one in command.

options.text: The locusts acting on their own instinct.
options.note: The army moves under God's command, not by mere instinct.

options.text: No one; the chaos is leaderless and random.
options.note: The passage stresses God's sovereign command over the host.

quiz.q: What is the effect of Joel piling up similes (like horses, like chariots, like fire)?

options.text: To overwhelm the reader with the dread and inevitability of the Day.
options.note: The barrage of images is meant to make the Day feel real, near, and terrifying.

options.text: To give a precise field report of the army's equipment.
options.note: The similes create dread, not a literal inventory.

options.text: To vividly convey the speed and force of the advance without exact detail.
options.note: They do convey speed and force, in service of overwhelming dread.

options.text: To soften the scene and reassure the reader.
options.note: The imagery heightens fear rather than easing it.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament use the darkening of sun, moon, and stars?

options.text: Jesus applies it to the signs of His return, and darkness fell at His crucifixion.
options.note: Matthew 24:29 and the darkness at the cross draw on this Day-of-the-LORD imagery.

options.text: It is treated as pure poetry with no later fulfillment.
options.note: The New Testament takes it up directly for the coming of Christ.

options.text: It appears in visions of the end, such as Revelation, as a sign of judgment.
options.note: True, and Jesus Himself also applies it to His return.

options.text: It is never mentioned again in Scripture.
options.note: The image recurs prominently in the Gospels and Revelation.

quiz.q: How does the closing question, 'Who can endure it?', point to Christ?

options.text: No one can endure the Day alone; Jesus endured it at the cross so His people can stand.
options.note: The question finds its answer in the One who bore the Day in our place.

options.text: It implies that strong and moral people will manage to endure on their own.
options.note: The point is that none can endure by their own strength or merit.

options.text: It leaves the reader with a real need that only God can meet.
options.note: True, and Scripture names Christ as the One who meets that need.

options.text: It shows the Day is not actually that serious.
options.note: The Day is great and very dreadful; the question underscores its gravity.

questions: Joel sounds the trumpet to shake a complacent people awake. What in your life has grown numb to the seriousness of God, and what would it take to hear the alarm?
The passage insists the Day of the LORD is real and coming. How does living with that reality in view change the way you spend today?
God Himself leads the army; even judgment obeys His command. How does His total sovereignty comfort you, and how does it sober you?
The chapter ends unanswered: who can endure it? Sit with that question honestly. Where are you tempted to think you could stand before God on your own record?
Jesus endured the Day of darkness so His people never will. How does knowing He faced the judgment in your place free you from the fear of the last Day?

translationNotes.note: BSB footnotes an alternative rendering, 'like charioteers' or 'like cavalry,' for the comparison to horses; the sense of swift, galloping advance is unchanged.
The rhetorical question that closes the section, 'Who can endure it?', is left deliberately open, setting up the call to return in verses 12-17.
